title: Tourism demand has recovered at scale, but geopolitical, climate, infrastructure, and host-community pressures are reshaping the sector
geography: OECD countries and partner-country profiles, with a United States country profile

observations.period: 2024-2025; OECD tourism aggregate and 2026 policy report

denominator.unit: international tourist arrivals to OECD countries in 2024; reported aggregate count

oecd_arrivals_growth_2024.unit: percent increase in international tourist arrivals to OECD countries in 2024

oecd_arrivals_2024.unit: international tourist arrivals to OECD countries in 2024

oecd_tourism_direct_gdp_share.unit: percent of GDP directly contributed by tourism in OECD countries, as summarized by the report

oecd_tourism_services_export_share.unit: percent of services exports directly associated with tourism in OECD countries, as summarized by the report

oecd_arrivals_growth_2025.unit: estimated percent growth in international arrivals to OECD countries in 2025

early_2026_shock.value: Middle East conflict disrupted travel flows and raised transport and other costs

observations.method: The OECD combines internationally comparable tourism statistics, country policy profiles, tourism governance evidence, and thematic analysis of social, environmental, digital, and resilience pressures.
observations.uncertainty: Tourist arrivals and tourism GDP do not measure visitor welfare, resident burden, job quality, local value retention, or environmental sustainability. 2025 growth is an estimate, and short-term geopolitical effects may differ across destinations and transport routes.
observations.subgroup: International visitors, destination residents and communities, tourism firms and workers, transport and retail suppliers, governments, and less-visited or high-pressure destinations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strong arrivals can support local income, cultural exchange, and regional development. Concentrated flows and shocks may be managed through visitor distribution, infrastructure investment, accessible tourism, data systems, and community participation rather than requiring demand reduction everywhere.

observations.period: 2023-2025; United States country profile in OECD Tourism Trends and Policies 2026

denominator.unit: United States tourism-economy percentage base; measure-specific reference years are stated in each measure

us_tourism_direct_gva_share_2023.unit: percent of U.S. total gross value added directly associated with tourism in 2023

us_tourism_direct_employment_share_2023.unit: percent of U.S. total employment directly associated with tourism in 2023

us_travel_exports_share_services_2025.unit: percent of U.S. services exports represented by travel exports in 2025

us_international_arrivals_2025.unit: international tourist arrivals to the United States in 2025

us_arrivals_change_2025.unit: percent change in U.S. international tourist arrivals from 2024 to 2025

us_arrivals_vs_2019.unit: percent of 2019 U.S. international tourist arrival level reached in 2025

us_domestic_person_trips_2025.unit: estimated domestic tourism person-trips in the United States in 2025

observations.method: The OECD country profile reports U.S. tourism output, employment, travel exports, international arrivals, domestic person-trips, governance, and policy priorities using national tourism statistics and the OECD comparative framework.
observations.uncertainty: The U.S. profile combines different statistical concepts and reference years; person-trips are not unique travelers, and arrival changes do not identify the contribution of visa rules, prices, safety perceptions, airline capacity, exchange rates, or geopolitical events.
observations.subgroup: U.S. domestic and international travelers, destination communities, tourism businesses, workers, transport systems, and federal, state, and local tourism authorities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower international arrivals can coexist with strong domestic travel and a large tourism economy. A decentralized policy structure can allow local experimentation, but may also make national-local coordination and impact distribution harder to observe.

boundary: This record adds a tourism demand, place-pressure, host-community, infrastructure, and geopolitical-resilience route. It does not measure individual travel motives, resident sentiment, tourism worker quality, local housing displacement, visitor welfare, or causal effects of any policy or conflict.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: OECD Tourism Trends and Policies 2026 executive summary, official PDF, and United States country profile retrieved; arrival, economic-share, export, domestic-trip, geopolitical-pressure, governance, and resilience claims cross-checked against the publication.
